---
title: "Quiz: normalisation and moment invariants"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. $\mu_{pq}$: central moments; $\eta_{pq} = \mu_{pq}/\mu_{00}^{1 + (p+q)/2}$; complex moments $c_{pq} = \sum (x + iy)^p (x - iy)^q I$ in central coordinates with $y$ up; Hu's $\phi_1, \dots, \phi_7$.

---

**Q1.** An object is moved 10 pixels to the right. Which change: $m_{10}$, $m_{20}$, $\mu_{20}$, $\eta_{30}$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which of them measure positions from the centroid?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$m_{10}$ and $m_{20}$ change (they measure from the image origin). $\mu_{20}$ and $\eta_{30}$ do not: central moments measure from the centroid, which moves with the object.
:::

---

**Q2.** An object is enlarged by a factor 2. By what factor do $\mu_{00}$, $\mu_{20}$ and $\mu_{30}$ change? And $\eta_{30}$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\mu'_{pq} = s^{p+q+2}\mu_{pq}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\mu_{00}$: $2^2 = 4$; $\mu_{20}$: $2^4 = 16$; $\mu_{30}$: $2^5 = 32$. $\eta_{30} = \mu_{30}/\mu_{00}^{5/2}$ changes by $32/4^{5/2} = 32/32 = 1$: not at all.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why is $\phi_1 = \eta_{20} + \eta_{02}$ unchanged by a rotation, while $\eta_{20}$ alone changes?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is $\eta_{20} + \eta_{02}$ in terms of the matrix $S$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It is the trace of the second-moment matrix (divided by $\mu_{00}^2$), i.e. the sum of its eigenvalues. A rotation turns the eigenvectors but keeps the eigenvalues. $\eta_{20}$ alone is the spread along the $x$-axis, which depends on how the object is turned.
:::

---

**Q4.** Of all shapes, the disc has the smallest $\phi_1$, namely $1/(2\pi) \approx 0.159$. A square has $1/6$. Without computing: is $\phi_1$ of a long thin rod larger or smaller than both?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\phi_1$ is the mean squared distance from the centroid, divided by the area.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Larger. For a fixed area, a rod has much of its mass far from the centroid, so its mean squared distance (relative to the area) is large. The disc packs the mass as close as possible: that is why it has the minimum.
:::

---

**Q5.** The object is rotated by 30° counter-clockwise. By how many degrees does the arrow of $c_{30}$ turn? Of $c_{12}$? Of $c_{11}$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$c_{pq} \to e^{i(p-q)\alpha} c_{pq}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$c_{30}$: $3 \cdot 30° = 90°$. $c_{12}$: $(1 - 2) \cdot 30° = -30°$ (backwards). $c_{11}$: 0°, it never turns.
:::

---

**Q6.** A shape has 3-fold rotational symmetry (it looks the same after a turn of 120°). Show that $c_{20} = 0$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Rotating by 120° gives the same image, so the same $c_{20}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Rotation by 120° multiplies $c_{20}$ by $e^{2i \cdot 120°} = e^{i \cdot 240°} \ne 1$. But the image, and so $c_{20}$, is unchanged. The only number with $c = e^{i240°} c$ is $c = 0$. (So $\phi_2 = 0$, and the orientation from the second moments is undefined.)
:::

---

**Q7.** You classify the letters b, d, p and q with Hu's invariants $\phi_1, \dots, \phi_6$. Which letters can you not tell apart? What changes if you add $\phi_7$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which pairs are rotations of each other, which are mirror images?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
b rotated by 180° is q; d rotated by 180° is p; b and d are mirror images. $\phi_1 \dots \phi_6$ are invariant under rotation and reflection, so all four look the same (up to font details). $\phi_7$ changes sign under reflection: it separates {b, q} from {d, p}, but not b from q.
:::

---

**Q8.** Why are Hu's invariants usually compared as $-\operatorname{sign}(\phi)\log_{10}|\phi|$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Typical values: $\phi_1 \approx 0.27$, $\phi_5 \approx -5 \times 10^{-7}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
They span many orders of magnitude (higher invariants are products of many small $\eta$'s). In a distance between feature vectors, $\phi_1$ would dominate and $\phi_5$ would not count at all. The log makes them comparable (0.58 and −6.27 here); the sign is kept because some invariants can be negative.
:::

---

**Q9.** Pose normalisation rotates the major axis of the object onto the $x$-axis. Name two shapes for which this fails, and say why.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The major axis is the eigenvector of $S$ with the larger eigenvalue.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A disc, a square, a regular hexagon, a plus sign, a 3-pointed star: all have $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2$, so every direction is a principal axis and the angle is undefined (and for nearly round objects, it is dominated by noise). A rectangle has a major axis but $\mu_{30} = 0$: the 180° ambiguity cannot be fixed by $\mu_{30}$.
:::

---

**Q10.** *(math)* Show that $c_{20} = \mu_{20} - \mu_{02} + 2i\mu_{11}$ and $c_{11} = \mu_{20} + \mu_{02}$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Expand $(x + iy)^2$ and $(x + iy)(x - iy)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$(x + iy)^2 = x^2 - y^2 + 2ixy$; summing with weights $I$ in central coordinates: $\mu_{20} - \mu_{02} + 2i\mu_{11}$. $(x + iy)(x - iy) = x^2 + y^2$, giving $\mu_{20} + \mu_{02}$. With $\eta$ instead of $\mu$: $|c_{20}|^2 = (\eta_{20} - \eta_{02})^2 + 4\eta_{11}^2 = \phi_2$ and $c_{11} = \phi_1$.
:::
